papers.title: Reconstitution of multistep recruitment of ULK1 to membranes in autophagy.
papers.summary: This paper reconstitutes in vitro the step-by-step process by which the ULK1 protein complex is recruited to membranes to initiate autophagy. It identifies the molecular signals and interactions that drive this multistep recruitment, clarifying how autophagy is triggered at the membrane level. This provides mechanistic insight into the earliest stages of autophagosome formation, a core process in cellular quality control.
papers.why: Understanding the core molecular machinery that initiates autophagy is directly relevant to studying mitophagy and autophagy pathways in neurons, even though this study uses a reconstituted non-neuronal system.

papers.title: Loss of RUBCN causes autophagy overdrive in a neurodevelopmental disorder with age-dependent neurodegeneration
papers.summary: This paper reports that loss of the RUBCN gene causes a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by excessive, unregulated autophagy, termed 'autophagy overdrive'. Patients with RUBCN mutations show developmental deficits early in life, followed by progressive neurodegeneration as they age. The findings suggest RUBCN normally acts as a brake on autophagy, and its loss disrupts the balance needed for healthy neuronal function over the lifespan.
papers.why: This directly relates to the mitophagy/autophagy dysregulation in neurons central to the PhD project, offering a genetic model of pathological autophagy overdrive with age-dependent neurodegeneration that could inform interneuron vulnerability and brain aging studies.

papers.title: Melatonin Improves Cognitive Function and Suppresses Excessive Mitophagy in Rats With Vascular Dementia.
papers.summary: This study tested melatonin in a rat model of vascular dementia, a condition caused by reduced blood flow to the brain. The researchers found that melatonin treatment improved the rats' cognitive performance while reducing signs of excessive mitophagy, the process by which cells clear damaged mitochondria. This suggests melatonin may protect neurons by keeping mitophagy at healthier, more balanced levels.
papers.why: This paper directly relates to the profile's focus on mitophagy in neurons and offers a disease-relevant model showing how excessive mitophagy can be pharmacologically modulated, which could inform mechanistic comparisons with the PhD project's neuronal and interneuron-focused work.

papers.title: Mitophagy: a regulator and therapeutic target in cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how mitophagy, the selective clearance of damaged mitochondria, influences brain damage after cerebral ischemia followed by reperfusion. It discusses the molecular pathways controlling mitophagy activation during this injury and how they affect neuronal survival or death. The review also highlights potential therapeutic strategies that target mitophagy to reduce stroke-related brain damage.
papers.why: Understanding mitophagy's regulatory mechanisms in neurons directly supports the project's core focus on mitophagy and autophagy in neurons in the brain, offering mechanistic context relevant to neuronal stress responses that could be mapped spatially.

papers.title: Mild Hypothermia Alleviates Ischemia and Reperfusion Injury by Activating PINK1/Parkin Mitophagy.
papers.summary: This study examines whether mild hypothermia can protect the brain from damage caused by ischemia and reperfusion, a process where blood flow is cut off then restored, often causing cellular harm. The researchers found that mild hypothermia works partly by activating PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy, a pathway that clears damaged mitochondria from cells. This activation appears to reduce injury and improve outcomes following ischemia and reperfusion events.
papers.why: Understanding how PINK1/Parkin mitophagy protects neurons under stress conditions like ischemia is directly relevant to studying mitophagy mechanisms in neurons that may also apply to interneuron vulnerability and resilience in the brain.

papers.title: Autophagy Deficits in Lower Motor Neuron and Striated Muscle Diseases: From Genetics to Therapeutic Advances.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how defects in autophagy—the cell's process for clearing damaged components—contribute to diseases affecting lower motor neurons and striated (skeletal) muscle. It covers the genetic mutations linked to autophagy dysfunction in these conditions and discusses emerging therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring proper autophagic function. The review connects basic molecular mechanisms to clinical translation for neuromuscular disorders.
papers.why: While focused on motor neurons and muscle rather than interneurons or perineuronal nets, this review offers useful genetic and mechanistic context on autophagy dysfunction in neuronal disease that could inform broader interpretive frameworks for the PhD project's mitophagy/autophagy focus.

papers.title: Amplification bias in sequencing-based spatial transcriptomics: sources, mechanisms, impacts, and mitigation strategies.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how amplification steps in sequencing-based spatial transcriptomics protocols can introduce biases into gene expression measurements. It covers where these biases come from technically, how they arise mechanistically during library preparation and sequencing, and what downstream effects they have on data quality and interpretation. The paper also discusses strategies to detect and correct for such biases to improve accuracy of spatial transcriptomic datasets.
papers.why: Since the PhD project relies on spatial transcriptomics to study neurons and perineuronal nets, understanding amplification bias is essential for correctly interpreting gene expression data and avoiding misleading conclusions.

papers.title: Impact of aging and caloric restriction on markers of mitochondrial dynamics, biogenesis, mitophagy, and autophagy in multiple metabolically active tissues
papers.summary: This paper examines how aging and caloric restriction affect molecular markers related to mitochondrial dynamics, biogenesis, mitophagy, and autophagy across several tissues with high metabolic demands. It likely compares young versus aged animals, with and without caloric restriction, to see how these cellular maintenance pathways change over time. The goal is to understand whether caloric restriction can preserve or restore healthy mitochondrial turnover and quality control mechanisms during aging.
papers.why: Understanding how mitophagy and autophagy markers shift with aging and metabolic intervention in peripheral tissues could inform comparative or mechanistic insights relevant to studying these same pathways in aging neurons and brain tissue.
